answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**A Plaintiff Need Not Plead a Prima Facie Case but Must Allege Facts Supporting a Plausible Inference of Discrimination.**

This Court reviews a Rule 12(b)(6) dismissal de novo, accepting well-pleaded facts as true and drawing reasonable inferences in the plaintiff's favor. *Goines v. Valley Cmty. Servs. Bd.*, 822 F.3d 159, 165–66 (4th Cir. 2016). The complaint must "state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face." *Ashcroft v. Iqbal*, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009) (quoting *Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly*, 550 U.S. 544, 570 (2007)).

**A. The prima facie case is an evidentiary standard, not a pleading requirement.**

The prima facie case under *McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green*, 411 U.S. 792 (1973), "is an evidentiary standard, not a pleading requirement." *Swierkiewicz v. Sorema N.A.*, 534 U.S. 506, 510 (2002). That framework presupposes an evidentiary record that does not yet exist when a complaint is filed, and discovery may reveal direct evidence that makes the framework unnecessary. *See id.* at 511–12.

After *Twombly* and *Iqbal*, this Court continues to hold that a Title VII plaintiff need not plead facts establishing a prima facie case to survive a motion to dismiss. *McCleary-Evans v. Md. Dep't of Transp., State Highway Admin.*, 780 F.3d 582, 584–85 (4th Cir. 2015); *see also Woods v. City of Greensboro*, 855 F.3d 639, 647–48 (4th Cir. 2017) (applying the same principle to a race discrimination claim under 42 U.S.C. § 1981). A court therefore should not dismiss a complaint merely because it does not establish each *McDonnell Douglas* component as a plaintiff might have to at summary judgment.

**B. The complaint must allege facts that make discrimination plausible.**

Freedom from the evidentiary framework does not relieve a plaintiff of Rule 8's demands. Even before *Twombly*, this Court explained that although a plaintiff need not plead facts sufficient to prove her case, she must allege facts that support each element of her claim. *Bass v. E.I. DuPont de Nemours & Co.*, 324 F.3d 761, 764–65 (4th Cir. 2003). Those allegations must "raise a right to relief above the speculative level." *Twombly*, 550 U.S. at 555; *see McCleary-Evans*, 780 F.3d at 585. Legal conclusions and bare recitals of the elements receive no presumption of truth. *Francis v. Giacomelli*, 588 F.3d 186, 193 (4th Cir. 2009).

A complaint accordingly fails when it rests on a conclusory assertion that race or sex motivated the employer. In *McCleary-Evans*, the plaintiff alleged that she was passed over in favor of non-Black candidates but offered only speculation that the decisionmakers acted because of race or sex. 780 F.3d at 585–86. Likewise, *Coleman v. Maryland Court of Appeals*, 626 F.3d 187, 190–91 (4th Cir. 2010), *aff'd on other grounds sub nom. Coleman v. Court of Appeals of Md.*, 566 U.S. 30 (2012), affirmed dismissal where conclusory allegations did not plausibly show that the plaintiff's termination was based on race. The elements of the claim thus inform the plausibility analysis, but the question remains whether the pleaded facts support the required inference, not whether the plaintiff has already proved it.

Plausibility is not probability. *Iqbal*, 556 U.S. at 678. A plaintiff need not show that discrimination is the likeliest explanation or rule out every lawful alternative; she must nudge her claim across the line from conceivable to plausible. *See Houck v. Substitute Tr. Servs., Inc.*, 791 F.3d 473, 484 (4th Cir. 2015). *Woods* illustrates the point: this Court reversed dismissal where the factual allegations permitted a reasonable inference of race discrimination. 855 F.3d at 649–52. Assessing that inference is "a context-specific task" drawing on "judicial experience and common sense." *Iqbal*, 556 U.S. at 679.

**C. [Plaintiff]'s allegations meet this standard.**

The question is whether, accepting [Plaintiff]'s factual allegations as true and reading them together, it is plausible that [Defendant] took the challenged action because of [protected characteristic]. It is. [Plaintiff] alleges [specific facts, e.g., discriminatory remarks, more favorable treatment of identified coworkers, departures from policy, or suspicious timing]. (J.A. __.) Those are concrete facts, not labels. Whether they ultimately prove discrimination is a question for a developed record. Requiring that proof now would reimpose the kind of heightened pleading requirement *Swierkiewicz* rejected. The judgment of dismissal should be reversed.
